title: A high win rate is not an edge: fair spreads have zero expected value
summary: A 10-wide debit call spread on Lululemon costs about $3.40 and can lose $6.60. Roughly two thirds of the time it makes about 50% in a month. The expected value comes out near zero: the market prices it fairly. A 70% win rate is the price of admission, not an edge. The edge must come from a view that differs from what the market already prices.

params.label: Excess drift over rate
params.help: Your view of annual return above the risk-free rate. Zero = the market view; EV is then about zero.

steps.caption: The market's price distribution for the stock one month out.
The one standard deviation band from implied volatility.
A 10-wide in-the-money call spread breaks even below the market.
About two thirds of the outcomes end above the short strike and earn the maximum, about 50% on the debit.
Weigh wins and losses by probability: the expected value is about zero. The trade is fairly priced.
Change the drift to your own view. Only a view different from the market's makes the expected value positive.

takeaways: A high win rate is the price of admission, not an edge.
The probability of max profit is roughly the delta of the short leg.
At fair prices the expected value of a vertical spread is about zero.
Start with a view. Use option leverage only when conviction is high: risk first, invest second, option overlays third.
caveats: The transcript does not give the Lululemon price or strikes; the chart uses example values with a 10-wide spread.
The example is educational and not a trade recommendation.
